title: DHS Proposes Ending Deference on Visa Extensions, Affecting About 208,000 Petitions a Year
excerpt: A one-sentence proposed rule would delete the regulation requiring USCIS to defer to its prior approvals on Form I-129 extensions — and DHS's own data says the main effect would be about 6,000 more evidence requests a year, not more denials.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has proposed deleting the regulation that requires USCIS to defer to its own earlier approval when an employer extends a worker's status on Form I-129.
  • DHS estimates about 208,000 petitions a year currently receive deference; H-1B petitions make up more than 75% of I-129 filings, and 77.6% of H-1B approvals for continuing employment in fiscal 2025 went to workers born in India.
  • DHS's own comparison found denial rates did not change in years without deference — the measurable effect was more Requests for Evidence: about 6,044 additional RFEs a year, each adding roughly 64 days to processing.
  • Nothing has changed yet: the comment period closed on November 13, 2026, and the current deference rule stays in force unless DHS publishes a final rule.

If your employer has already won approval for your H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN or E petition once, a routine extension for the same worker in the same job is today a comparatively predictable filing. Under 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) must generally defer to its earlier determination when the parties and the underlying facts are the same, departing from it only for a material error, a material change, or new adverse information. A proposed rule published by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on October 14, 2026 would delete that paragraph entirely.

Who is affected — exactly

The proposal, titled "Removing Deference to Prior USCIS Determinations of Eligibility" (91 FR 65119; DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0529), covers every extension filed on Form I-129, the petition employers use for nonimmigrant workers. The classifications named in the proposal include H-1B, H-1B1, L-1, O-1, O-2, TN, E-1, E-2, E-3, H-2A, H-2B, H-3, P, Q-1 and R-1 workers. It does not change initial petitions, change-of-status filings, or the underlying eligibility rules for any category — it changes only the weight an officer must give a previous approval. New applicants are not affected; the change bites at renewal time, typically three years into a job.

Counted in DHS's estimate of about 208,429 affected petitions a year: extension requests that currently qualify for deference because the employer, worker and facts are unchanged. Not counted: first-time petitions and extensions involving a new employer or materially changed role, which are already reviewed fresh. H-1B holders would feel the change most. According to The American Bazaar, DHS notes that H-1B petitions account for more than 75% of all I-129 filings, and USCIS data for fiscal 2025 shows 77.6% of H-1B approvals for continuing employment went to India-born workers.

What would change, precisely

Today, deference is the officer's starting point: the earlier approval stands unless the officer identifies a specific reason it should not. The proposal removes that starting point. As immigration attorney Bhumireddy Sai Srinivas Reddy told The American Bazaar, the proposed rule "is only one sentence long," but "officers could still consider a prior approval — it would no longer be their starting point." Employers would carry the full burden of proving eligibility again on every extension, as the statute places that burden on the petitioner.

"The Department of Homeland Security has published a proposed rule that is only one sentence long."

— Bhumireddy Sai Srinivas Reddy, immigration attorney, to The American Bazaar

DHS gives three reasons for the change, according to the notice: the law places the burden of proof on the employer, and deference effectively shifts it to the officer; the practice discourages officers from requesting additional evidence when a petition raises questions; and an erroneous initial approval can become an "anchor," carrying mistakes or fraud into later filings. The department put the added cost to petitioners at about $134,000 a year.

What DHS's own data shows

The department compared years with and without deference and found that denial rates did not change. The only measurable effect of removing deference was an increase in Requests for Evidence (RFEs) — DHS estimates roughly 6,044 additional RFEs a year, a rise of about 2.9 percentage points in the RFE rate. "In other words, the government expects the same cases to be approved in the end, but only after more paperwork and longer waits," Reddy said. DHS estimates an RFE adds about 64 days to processing. That matters against a hard deadline: an H-1B worker whose employer has timely filed an extension can generally keep working for up to 240 days after their authorized stay expires while the petition is pending, so slower processing pushes more workers closer to that limit.

When, and what to do now

The public comment period closed on November 13, 2026; The American Bazaar reported that 1,780 submissions were received. DHS must review the comments before it can publish a final rule, which could differ from the proposal and would set its own effective date. Until then, the deference regulation remains in force and officers must still apply it — no filing strategy changes today. Analyses of the proposal advise employers and workers not to withdraw, re-file or delay any petition because of a proposal. What to watch: publication of a final rule in the Federal Register under docket USCIS-2026-0529, and any litigation challenging it. For workers with an extension due in the next year, the practical step is the unglamorous one — make sure the employer's evidence file (role, wages, worksite, credentials) is complete enough to prove eligibility from scratch, because that is the review a final rule would require.
